One thing before the draft, because it matters for *you*: a compliance statement lands best when it states facts and lets the reviewer draw the conclusion. If you write "I had no audit obligation" as a flat assertion, you're making a policy claim that compliance will go check against your role's procedures — and if there's any language anywhere about spot-checks or secondary review, that sentence becomes the thing they fixate on. Saying "I relied on AP's written clearance, consistent with the standard process" gets you to the same place, but it's a factual claim you can back up with the email. It's stronger, not weaker.

Based on that written clearance, I signed off on the batches and executed the push on [date/time]. This followed the standard workflow for my role, in which [role/team] executes batches after AP has completed its scrub and issued clearance. I did not perform an independent review of the batch contents, as AP's clearance is the control point for that step under the normal process, and I had no indication at the time that the clearance was incomplete or that anything in the batches warranted additional review.

I became aware of the issue on [date] when [how you found out]. Since then I have [any steps: preserved the email, stopped further pushes, notified X, etc.].

I am available to provide the original clearance email, batch logs, and any other records related to this matter.

[Name, title, date]
